idiom_name: enum tag + union payload nodes interpreted by one eval() switch (or a function-pointer dispatch table)
implementation_notes: C has no sum types, closures or generics, so the operation algebra is hand-written: an `enum kind` tag, a `struct node` with a union payload, and one allocating constructor per operation. The interpreter is a single recursive `eval(node *, env *)` switching on the tag; where the switch cost matters, an array of `double (*)(const struct node *, struct env *)` handlers indexed by kind gives the same dispatch with direct jumps. Nothing in the language replaces this structure - this *is* the pattern, expressed as tagged data plus a separate evaluator - and that separation is exactly what lets the same program feed an evaluator, a printer or a cost model. The classic form stays justified for small instruction or expression sets; once operations and invariants multiply, a bytecode compiler or a generated interpreter is the honest upgrade.
pitfalls: The union is untyped: reading a member that does not belong to the current tag is undefined behaviour, so every access must go through the switch and the tag is part of the node's contract.
Nodes are heap-allocated and nothing frees them: use an arena owned by the program or a recursive free after interpretation, otherwise every run leaks.
C has no exhaustiveness check: `-Wswitch` warns about a missing enum case only when there is no `default`, so keep a default arm that aborts or returns an error instead of silently returning 0.
